### 1.  A convenient recurrence

Denote  

\[
S_n=\{x\in\mathbb N:\;x>a_{\,n-1},\;x\equiv n\pmod K\}.
\]

\(S_n\) is an arithmetic progression:
\[
S_n=\{t_n,\;t_n+K,\;t_n+2K,\dots\},
\]
where  

\[
t_n=\min\{x>a_{\,n-1}:x\equiv n\pmod K\}
\]

is the **first** element of \(S_n\).  
Since we need the \(n\)-th element of \(S_n\),

\[
a_n=t_n+(n-1)K.    \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The first element is always \(a_{n-1}+1\)

We claim that for every \(n\ge 2\)

\[
t_n=a_{n-1}+1,
\qquad\text{equivalently }a_{n-1}+1\equiv n\pmod K.   \tag{2}
\]

**Proof by induction.**  

*Base case \(n=1\):* \(a_1=1\) and \(1\equiv1\pmod K\); (2) holds for \(n=2\) because
\(a_1+1=2\equiv2\pmod K\).

*Inductive step.* Assume \(a_{n-1}\equiv n-1\pmod K\). Then  

\[
a_{n-1}+1\equiv (n-1)+1\equiv n\pmod K .
\]

Since \(a_{n-1}+1>a_{n-1}\), it is a member of \(S_n\). No smaller integer \(>a_{n-1}\) can be in \(S_n\), hence it is the smallest element, i.e. \(t_n=a_{n-1}+1\). ∎

Consequently the distance from \(a_{n-1}\) to the first appropriate number is always \(1\); the “skipping’’ comes only from the \( (n-1)K\) term in (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The simple recurrence for \(a_n\)

Substituting \(t_n=a_{n-1}+1\) into (1) gives

\[
a_n=a_{n-1}+1+(n-1)K,\qquad n\ge2,
\]
or

\[
a_n-a_{n-1}=K(n-1)+1. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Solving the recurrence

Sum (3) for \(j=2,\dots ,n\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_n
&=a_1+\sum_{j=2}^{n}\bigl(K(j-1)+1\bigr)                              \\
&=1+K\sum_{i=1}^{\,n-1}i +(n-1)                                         \\
&=1+K\frac{(n-1)n}{2}+(n-1).
\end{aligned}
\]

Simplifying,

\[
a_n=\frac{K n^2-(K-2)n}{2}
      =\frac{K\,n(n-1)+2n}{2}
      =\frac{K n^2-(K-2)n}{2}. \tag{4}
\]

Because \(n(n-1)\) is always even, the numerator in (4) is divisible by \(2\), so \(a_n\) is an integer for every \(n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Final explicit formula

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle a_n=\frac{K n^{2}-(K-2)n}{2}
      \qquad (n\ge1).}
\]

One can check that this formula reproduces the defining property:
\[
a_{n-1}+1\equiv n\pmod K,\qquad 
a_n=a_{n-1}+1+(n-1)K,
\]
so \(a_n\) is indeed the \(n\)-th natural number larger than \(a_{n-1}\) congruent to \(n\pmod K\).  
For example:

* \(K=2\): \(a_n=n^{2}\) (the squares);
* \(K=3\): \(a_n=\frac{3n^{2}-n}{2}=n\bigl(3n-1\bigr)/2\);
* \(K=4\): \(a_n=n(2n-1)\);
* \(K=1\): \(a_n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\) (triangular numbers).

Thus the explicit expression (4) solves the problem for any positive integer \(K\).<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>
